scenes.note: Your face shows. This is the hook, so lift your energy and look at the camera.
lines: Right. Watch this cell. I'm going to lift the salt bridge out, and the current drops to zero. Straight away.
But the electrons don't even go through the salt bridge. They go through the wire. So what was that little tube actually doing? That's today's question.

scenes.note: Voice over the board. Slow and clear.
lines: Look at the zinc half-cell first. Zinc atoms keep turning into zinc two plus ions, so positive charge builds up in that solution.
Now the copper side. Copper two plus ions are being removed, because they're turning into copper. The nitrate ions get left behind, so negative charge builds up there.
That build-up of charge pushes back against the flow. Within seconds, the current stops.

scenes.note: Your face shows. Ask the question, then stay quiet for 3 seconds before the answer. The lesson stops there for the learner.
lines: Your turn to think. The salt bridge is potassium nitrate. Which ions move out of the bridge into the zinc half-cell? Pause the lesson and write it down.
The nitrate ions. They're negative, so they move into the zinc half-cell, where positive charge is building up.
And at the same time, potassium ions move into the copper half-cell, where copper two plus ions are being removed. Ions from each half-cell move into the bridge too. So ions move both ways.

scenes.note: Voice over the board. Exam voice: this is where the marks are.
lines: Now, how do you get the marks? The memo wants two functions. One: it completes the circuit. Two: it maintains electrical neutrality in the half-cells.
If you have to describe it, name the ions and name the half-cells. Just writing that ions flow through the salt bridge gets you nothing on its own.

scenes.note: Your face shows. Lean in a little. This is the warning.
lines: Here's the one I see in every test. Electrons do not go through the salt bridge. Ever. Electrons stay in the wire and the electrodes. In the solutions and in the bridge, it's ions that carry the charge.

scenes.note: Voice over the lab. Steady pace.
lines: Last thing: which salt do we use? The ions in the bridge must not react with either half-cell. That's why potassium nitrate is the usual choice. Nitrates don't form precipitates.

Potassium chloride won't work next to a silver half-cell. The chloride ions react with the silver ions to form a white precipitate of silver chloride, and that removes silver ions from the cathode half-cell.
Next to a permanganate half-cell it fails for a different reason. Permanganate is a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine, so it oxidises the chloride ions.

scenes.note: Your face shows. Warm finish, smile, point them to the lab.
lines: Over to you. Open the galvanic cell lab, change the salt bridge, and watch what each choice does to the voltage. Then do the check questions. See you there.

roomTone.note: Sit still and say nothing for 10 seconds. I use this to take out the background hum.
